title: Light, Spectra and What Starlight Tells Us

cards.h: We cannot visit stars, so light is everything
cards.b: The nearest star beyond the Sun is 4.2 light-years away. No probe will visit in our lifetimes. Yet we know what stars are made of, how hot they are, how fast they move and how they spin. All of it comes from one thing: the light that reaches us.

Light is an electromagnetic wave. Its wavelength sets its type: radio (metres), microwave, infrared, visible (about 400 nm violet to 700 nm red), ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays (tiny).

All travel at the same speed in vacuum: 299,792 km/s. Our eyes see only a thin slice. Astronomers need all of it, because different processes glow in different bands.

Every hot object glows with a smooth rainbow whose peak colour depends on temperature: hotter means bluer. This is blackbody radiation. A red giant (about 3,500 K) looks orange-red; the Sun (about 5,800 K) looks yellow-white; a hot star (above 10,000 K) looks blue-white.

Hotter also means far more power: total output goes as temperature to the fourth power (Stefan, 1879).

cards.h: Spectral lines: a barcode of elements
cards.b:
Pass starlight through a prism or grating and you spread it into a spectrum. Dark gaps, called absorption lines, appear at precise colours. Each element and molecule absorbs only its own colours, like a fingerprint.

Joseph von Fraunhofer mapped hundreds of dark lines in sunlight in 1814. In 1859 Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that each line belongs to a chemical element. Suddenly we could do chemistry on the Sun.

Stars are sorted by line patterns into types O, B, A, F, G, K, M from hottest to coolest. The Sun is G. Annie Jump Cannon built this scheme around 1900. Cecilia Payne then showed in 1925 that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, and that the line patterns differ because of temperature, not composition.

If a source moves toward us its waves are squeezed: blueshift. If it moves away they are stretched: redshift. The size of the shift gives the speed along the line of sight: v/c = shift in wavelength divided by original wavelength.

It reveals binary stars, orbiting planets, spinning galaxies and, as we will see, the expansion of the universe.

cards.h: Helium was found in the Sun first
cards.b: During the total solar eclipse of 18 August 1868, the French astronomer Pierre Janssen saw an unfamiliar bright yellow line in the Sun's edge from Guntur in India. Norman Lockyer saw it too; he named the new element helium after the Greek Sun. It was found on Earth only in 1895. A new element discovered 150 million km away.

• 'A star's colour is its composition.' Colour tracks temperature.
  • 'Redshift means the object looks red.' It means its wavelengths are stretched; the object may remain white.
  • 'Light always travels at c.' Only in vacuum. In glass or water it slows down.

In 1920 Meghnad Saha derived the Saha ionisation equation, showing how a star's temperature and pressure decide which atoms lose electrons. This explained why star types differ and became a foundation of astrophysics.

C.V. Raman discovered in 1928 that light scattered by molecules changes colour slightly, the Raman effect, used today to identify materials (Nobel Prize 1930). And the 1868 helium line was first seen from Guntur, Andhra Pradesh.

• All astronomy is decoding light across the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Colour gives temperature; hotter stars are bluer and much brighter.
  • Spectral lines act as element fingerprints.
  • Doppler shifts give motion along the line of sight.

Think about it: (1) Why do two stars of the same temperature but different size have the same colour but different brightness? (2) How could you tell a star is spinning from its spectrum?

quiz.q: Dark absorption lines in starlight tell us about:
o: Chemical elements in the star's atmosphere
